implementation_notes: Keep `private final List<Course> courses = new ArrayList<>();` and return `Collections.unmodifiableList(courses)`: the JDK documents it as an unmodifiable view whose query operations 'read through' to the list and whose mutators throw UnsupportedOperationException. The wrapper is cheap (one object, cacheable in a field) and live - Oracle's guidance stresses it is 'not actually immutable' because the owner's own changes remain visible. Mutators are addCourse/removeCourse (plus an explicit replaceAll when bulk replacement is real).
pitfalls: The view is live: a caller that iterates it while the owner adds an element can get ConcurrentModificationException - document view vs snapshot, or hand out a copy.
The view is not deep: elements are shared, so mutating a Course remains visible through the unmodifiable list.
Sorting the view (Collections.sort) throws UnsupportedOperationException; ordering is an owner operation, not a client one.
Publishing the concrete field type (ArrayList) or a package-private field reopens mutation - the declared type should be List/Set/Collection, never the implementation.

variants.name: List.copyOf unmodifiable snapshot (Java 10)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 10's `List.copyOf(courses)` returns an unmodifiable snapshot: the specification promises that later modification of the source 'will not reflect such modifications', and Oracle's tutorial distinguishes it from the unmodifiable view - copyOf isolates the returned collection instead of reading through. Prefer it when the collection leaves the owner's thread, is cached, or is iterated while the owner may keep writing; the live view above stays cheaper when readers must observe updates.
pitfalls: A copy per call allocates: on a hot read path cache the snapshot and invalidate it in the mutators (or use an immutable backing collection).
List.copyOf rejects null elements (NPE) unlike ArrayList - an owner that tolerates nulls must filter or keep using the wrapper.
The snapshot is shallow: it fixes membership at copy time, not the state of the elements.
